THE COUNTER IS NEVER A STRIP ALONG THE BOTTOM OF THE FRAME WITH ALL THREE FIGURES BEHIND IT — that is what makes the gentlemen read as bartenders — and it is NEVER a table, a booth, a desk or a ledge: it is the bar's own slab, and the gentlemen are its patrons.

FARTHEST, PAST THE COUNTER, THE SERVICE SIDE: first the counter's FAR EDGE drawn as its own clean marble line beyond the drinks, then the walkway, then the back bar with its bottles and mirror, the television above it, the chalkboard beside — and ABBY when she is named, facing them, THE COUNTER'S FAR EDGE CROSSING HER AT THE WAIST and hiding her below it; she stands and they sit, so HER HEAD SITS HIGHER IN THE FRAME THAN THEIRS.

The two of them are on one side and she is on the other, always, and they never swap. When it is ambiguous the prop settles it: ANY LIQUOR BOTTLE OR BAR TOWEL IN THE PANEL IS ABBY'S — in her hands or on her shoulder — never in theirs. A stemmed glass has exactly ONE bowl on ONE stem on ONE foot — never a doubled stem, never two feet, never a second outline behind the hand. Every prop rests ON the marble or in a closed grip — nothing floats, nothing merges or clips. A LIFTED GLASS LEAVES ITS NAPKIN AND COASTER FLAT ON THE MARBLE: nothing sticks to the foot of a raised glass.

DREW. Preserve Drew exactly as the reference plates draw him (canon/vision/drew-plate1-bar-reference.jpg is the definitive study — the bar Drew of plate 1, with the LONG graceful high S-curve neck and the SMALL refined head; never a short thick neck, never a hunched or heavy bird. HIS BILL IS SLENDER, AND THE BLACK IS A MARKING ON IT RATHER THAN A PART OF IT. Two rules decide the shape, and they are the two the drawing keeps getting wrong.

FIRST, DEPTH. The bill is SLENDER: where it meets the feathers, its depth top-to-bottom is about ONE THIRD of its length. It tapers from there to the tip. Take the shape from a SWAN: a slender bill of even taper, bending in one gentle unbroken curve, with a small dark patch at the very tip. Its length is not the problem — a long slender bill is right; a thick one is wrong.

HIS BILL IS SLENDER AND IT DOES NOT BREAK. It leaves the face tucked and close, drops STEEPLY and STRAIGHT, and continues its own single curve smoothly to a ROUNDED TIP — one unbroken line from base to tip with no angle, no elbow, no kink and no hook anywhere along it. LAY A RULER ALONG THE UNDERSIDE AND IT SHOULD TOUCH ALMOST THE WHOLE LENGTH. The tip never hangs below the line the bill was already travelling on, and it never widens into a deep spoon. The rear two thirds are PALE; along the OUTER THIRD ONLY, the black IS the outline — it continues the bill's own curve rather than swelling into a bulb — with one bright highlight ribbon inside it. The NOSTRIL is a plain thin slit about HALF the length of his eye, with NO ring, outline or fleshy surround around it. There is no shelf or ridge above the eye.

He is FAR MORE FLAMINGO THAN HUMAN — plump, soft-bodied and FEATHERED ALL OVER in fine dash-strokes: breast, shoulders, back and arms, with long scalloped wing-feathers beneath each forearm. No human skin, torso, musculature or face anywhere; he is a bird who happens to sit at a bar. His neck is thick at the shoulders and rises in the deep question-mark sweep of a true flamingo, turning over at the top so the head hangs forward of where the neck left the body. His eyes are heavy-lidded and deadpan — visible white, distinct dark iris and pupil, a drooping upper lid and one fine contour line above it — never a bird dot. His face is AMIABLE: plump, softly modelled cheeks and a faint smile-line, a man who has heard it before and is fond of you anyway; never gaunt, hollow-eyed, sunken or sinister.

NO HAND IN THIS PANEL HAS A NAIL ON IT. Not Drew's, not Barclay's, not Abby's: every fingertip in the picture ends BLUNT AND SOFT in fur, plumage or pad, and a drawn nail, claw, talon or crescent at any fingertip is a redraw wherever it appears. THE ONLY HUMANLIKE THING ABOUT HIM IS HIS HANDS. Each feathered arm ends in a genuine hand — four slender fingers and an opposed thumb, feather-covered to the tips, elegant on a martini stem. WHITE PLUMAGE RUNS UNBROKEN FROM SHOULDER TO FINGERTIP: no sleeve, no cuff, no hem, no seam anywhere on the arm, and nothing smooth or bare-skinned anywhere on him. A crisp starched WHITE collar band circles the base of his neck and his small solid-black silk bow tie sits at the throat in front of it. DRAW THE TIE AS A TIED BOW: TWO wings of equal size spreading left and right, each wider at its outer edge, pinched to a SMALL CENTRE KNOT; horizontal, level, centred under the chin, resting ON the collar. Never one lump, never tilted, never more than two wings. THE BOW IS THE ONLY BLACK AT HIS NECK — no band, ribbon, strap, cord or choker runs around it or behind the bow. He wears a V-neck knitted sweater vest in fine honeycomb stitch with ribbed edges over a pale collared shirt, and trousers; THE VEST IS PLAIN KNIT WITH NO POCKETS ANYWHERE — none on the front, and never a pocket, flap or panel on the back. His plumage is pale but hatched — fine dash-strokes over white, high midtone rather than bare paper. At the bar his martini is always within reach: conical stemmed glass, ONE olive on ONE pick, on a napkin or coaster, held by the stem when lifted. His seat is frame-left, neck arched so his face hangs where the gag needs it. WHEN THIS SCENE HAS DREW SPEAKING his bill is SLIGHTLY PARTED, caught mid-word — never a clamped-shut bill on the one who is talking. At golf he adds a visor; a monocle is an approved occasional accessory.

BARCLAY. A successful gentleman in his mid-forties, unmistakably a golden retriever, drawn like one (canon/vision/barclay-reference.jpg is the definitive study): fur layered in fine individual strokes, drop ears with long fringe, broad soft-eyed retriever face, freckled muzzle, true black dog lips, dark lip-line along the muzzle from under his black nose, chest ruff modest, never a heavy neck-beard; middle-aged, solid, rounded shoulders, modest belly, absolutely no tail. HIS MOUTH IS CLOSED IN EVERY PANEL — never hanging open, never panting, never a visible tongue, never bared teeth. Default read: worried, earnest everyman against Drew's deadpan — BUT HE IS NOT SAD, and the first glance must not read as sad. Worry in the BROWS ONLY: raised inner brows, faint forehead wrinkle. Below the brows all WARM: mouth corners gently UP into a soft closed-lip smile, eyes bright and open, a clear catchlight in each, cheeks full and lifted. Read: a good-humoured man a little concerned, never a downcast one: mouth up, brows up, eyes bright. Hands visibly a dog's: broad, fur-backed, soft-padded fingers, NO NAILS OR CLAWS DRAWN AT ALL, each fingertip ending in soft fur and pad, never in a nail, yet fully humanoid in articulation: four fingers and an opposed thumb, believable human grips. At the bar, his dark suit jacket over a pale open-collared shirt, no tie; for daytime, travel, golf, a pale collared polo, dark leather belt, (outdoors) a ball cap; at golf his bag stands at frame-right, towel on its front hand-lettered in three lines FORE! / NOT SO / FAST. The small USA flag pin is PERMANENT: left lapel when jacketed, left chest of shirt or polo otherwise; on whatever he wears. A wristwatch on his left wrist in every panel EXCEPT at golf: a white golf glove on his left hand takes its place on that same wrist, smooth, unfurred to the cuff, forearm above it still furred; the watch and the glove are never both drawn, never on opposite sides of him. IN A BAR PANEL his old fashioned (short rocks glass, one large cube, one dark cherry) rests flat at frame-right, the shared bowl of bar nuts between the two drinks; AWAY FROM THE BAR he brings neither, whatever he holds belongs to the place he is in.

Drew and Barclay are gentlemen — classy, composed, well turned out; all three principals carry wisdom and command respect purely by how they carry themselves. Nothing about them is ever crude, sloppy or loud, and every scene carries that high-class read. Text inside the panel lives ON things and is a gag layer: whatever lettered surfaces THIS setting actually has — a chyron, a menu or scoreboard, a posted notice, a banner, a placard, a label — may each carry a short, legible, hand-lettered joke DRAWN FROM THE SAME JOKE as the caption, so the place and the line land as one gag from several angles. Letter ONLY the surfaces this setting genuinely has. No speech balloons, no thought bubbles, and no floating caption text inside the art — the dialogue is typeset by the house beneath the panel. THE SCENE: Barclay, earnest and resigned, swirls the ice in his old fashioned; Drew, deadpan, studies him over the rim of his martini; Abby, laughing, tops up the nut bowl in front of Barclay with a generous shake. IN THIS PANEL, CAMERA behind the two gentlemen on the CUSTOMER SIDE — their bodies block the counter's near edge — with ABBY working the FAR service side across the counter, the back bar behind HER alone. The television picture shows A gas pump with its nozzle hung in the cradle, the price display blank. Stage it exactly as THE SIDES describes. Abby is SMILING in this panel — an unmistakable smile, mouth corners up, eyes bright — NEVER sad, neutral or downcast; her beat is ACTIVE and cheerful: pouring, presenting a glass, laughing at her own line.

ABBY. Abby is the successful proprietor of The Swinging Door — a glamorous, feminine West Highland White Terrier in her mid-forties who owns the room and works its bar, drawn in the same engraved technique (canon/vision/abby-face-reference.jpg is the definitive face study): a true fluffy westie face in fine individual fur strokes, the head taken from a GROOMED SHOW WESTIE. HER FACE IS EXACTLY THE FACE OF HER STUDY, and wherever these words and that picture differ, THE PICTURE WINS. It is a small fluffy show-groomed head, ROUND AND SOFT: her big black nose sits DIRECTLY UNDER HER EYES on a round fluffy face — there is NO projecting muzzle to draw at all, no bridge, no cone, NO snout ever; nose, eyes and tiny closed smile all live on the front of one soft round head, and nothing sharp, foxish or wolfish appears anywhere. Her face reads SOFT, PRETTY, WARM and unmistakably FEMININE: long lashes, groomed brows, the fluff around her face shaped the way a stylist would leave it. HER EYES ARE HER BEST FEATURE AND THE MOST BEAUTIFUL THING IN THE PANEL. THEY ARE GLAMOROUS, LIDDED EYES, not a puppy's buttons: the upper lid sits low and sultry over the iris, the dark lash line is HEAVY and sweeps up and out at the corner, a bright catchlight sits high in each, and her look is warm, knowing and sidelong. Each is built like a HUMAN eye: a wide almond, WIDER THAN IT IS TALL, tilted up at the outer corner, white showing both sides of a drawn IRIS with a smaller round PUPIL. Draw them LARGE — EACH EYE AT LEAST AS WIDE AS THE BLACK OF HER NOSE — clear, bright and alert. Two or three fine brow strokes above each, two small pricked ears, and A SMILE IN EVERY PANEL — an unmistakable smile, mouth corners clearly UP and eyes bright, closed-lip or a happy open smile, whether she is at rest, serving or landing a line; a straight, neutral, pursed or downcast mouth on her is a redraw, as are drooping brows or mournful eyes. She is turned into the frame only as far as keeps BOTH EYES ON THE PAPER, the far eye at least half the width of the near one, the bridge of her muzzle showing between them. Her body is slightly humanoid, built exactly like the two gentlemen: upright on two legs, humanoid shoulders and arms, and fur-backed dog-yet-humanoid hands with soft pads and FOUR FINGERS AND AN OPPOSED THUMB, every finger separately drawn, closing on glass, towel and bottle neck in believable human grips. Trim, natural and graceful: a clean shoulder line and a waist the reader can find. HER FIGURE IS SLIM AND HER BUST IS SMALL AND NATURAL — the placket of her blouse runs very nearly STRAIGHT DOWN her front and the front reads as one gentle plane, never two separated volumes with a shadowed cleft between them. Her blouse is UNBUTTONED TWO BUTTONS DOWN so the collar falls open in a soft V, and the V falls open DEEP ENOUGH THAT THE SMOOTH CURVE OF HER CLEAVAGE SHOWS, drawn frankly attractive: throat, collarbone and the soft shadowed line between the curves, all reading as smooth skin. THE FUR IS WHAT SPOILS IT, so the long fur of her head and cheeks STOPS at her jawline and below it everything is SHORT, FINE and CLOSE-LYING — not one ruff, tuft or wisp of fluff breaks the clean line of the V. It is a LOWER NECKLINE, never a larger bust, and a shaggy chest inside an open collar is a redraw. She wears her fitted light blouse with rolled sleeves, a dark fitted skirt, a studded leather collar with a small teardrop gem pendant at its centre, a pearl bracelet and black heels; absolutely no tail. Her folded bar towel is ALWAYS SOMEWHERE IN THE PANEL, never missing from it, and in EXACTLY ONE PLACE AND NEVER BOTH: either draped over her LEFT SHOULDER with both hands empty of it, or held in her hands round the glass she is polishing with her shoulder BARE. There is only one towel in the panel. IN A BAR PANEL she works the service side directly across the marble from the gentlemen, standing to it on her own two feet with her arms free, visibly mid-task with ONE HAND CLOSED ON A WORKING OBJECT — glass, bottle, towel, chalk, or whatever THIS scene hands her; when the scene gives her its own object to handle, the towel rides her LEFT SHOULDER and both hands stay free of it — and the panel crops at the counter, its far edge cutting her at the waist and hiding her below it. AWAY FROM THE BAR she stands on the ground like everyone else, there on a named errand of the house, still with her towel and still with one hand busy, with no counter to stand behind, and the panel crops at whatever edge that setting names.

tv: TEN OF ELEVEN S&P SECTORS FALL TO OPEN SEPTEMBER
board: REGULAR, FRIDAY $61 / REGULAR, TUESDAY $74 / PAY AT THE PUMP
prompt:
Draw ONE single-panel black-and-white gag cartoon, one unbroken scene edge to edge — no seam, no split, no second frame, and no photographic rendering.

REFERENCES. @image1 is Drew, exactly as the studio's official portrait — copy THIS bird identically: the bill, the black bow tie, the knitted sweater vest, and the feathered hands with four fingers and a thumb and no claws. The cartoon's Drew must be indistinguishable from this one. @image2 is Barclay, exactly as the studio's official portrait — copy THIS dog identically: both eyes on the paper, the closed mouth, the flag pin on his left lapel, the wristwatch, the fur-backed clawless hands. The cartoon's Barclay must be indistinguishable from this one. @image3 is Abby, exactly as the studio's official portrait — copy THIS lady identically: the round soft head with the big black nose close under the eyes and no muzzle, the glamorous lidded eyes, the smooth open neckline, the studded collar with its gem, the towel. The cartoon's Abby must be indistinguishable from this one. @image4 is a FINISHED PANEL of this exact strip: the SAME room, the SAME cast in the SAME seats, poses and expressions, the same drinks on the same counter, the same window and shelves. COPY IT LINE FOR LINE — and change ONLY what the scene below orders: the television's picture and headline and the chalkboard's lettering, plus any detail this description names differently from the tile (bottle labels, taps, glassware, a smile). If this scene casts a character the tile does not show — Abby, on the FAR service side across the counter — ADD her exactly as described below without moving or redrawing anyone the tile already has. HER FACE IS THE FACE OF HER OWN PORTRAIT TILE, NOT INVENTED: a round, soft, fluffy show-westie head with NO muzzle or snout, big glamorous lidded eyes, a small black nose right under them, and a wide happy smile — nothing narrow, sharp, foxish or wolfish; a pointed face or a thin mouth on her is a redraw. Everything else stays exactly as the tile draws it, including the counter's panelled front face at frame-left. THE TELEVISION KEEPS ITS BROADCAST GRAMMAR exactly as the tile shows it — the CNBC LIVE bug, the ONE-LINE headline band across the bottom of the screen reading this scene's headline, and the time stamp; a screen showing only a picture with no headline band is a redraw. THE COUNTER'S TOP EDGE RUNS LEVEL across the picture — parallel to the bottom edge, the same height at Drew's window end as in front of him, never receding upward toward the window. FRAME THE ROOM EXACTLY AS THE TILE FRAMES IT: the television high on the wall with the whole chalkboard beside it, the marble counter with every glass and the nut bowl in the LOWER THIRD of the picture, and the TOPS OF BOTH STUDDED LEATHER CHAIR BACKS showing along the bottom edge, exactly as in the tile. Your canvas is taller than the tile: the BOTTOM SIXTH of your canvas will be trimmed away, so put nothing that matters there — only the lower parts of the two chair backs — and keep the counter, the drinks and the chair-back tops ABOVE that band. Draw each character exactly as his or her own reference draws that character — same face, same build, same wardrobe — and give the panel the same antique-engraving hand. Do NOT reproduce any reference's own background, signage, lettering, or composition: every word of lettering in this cartoon comes from the scene described below, and nothing else.

The finished panel contains EXACTLY 3 characters, each a separate individual — never merged, never duplicated, never omitted.

THE CARTOON:

A single-panel gag cartoon drawn like an antique steel engraving: fine pen crosshatching and stippling on every surface — wood grain, knit stitches, fur and feathers laid in individual strokes, glass catching light — with a full tonal range from deep rich blacks through silvery greys to bright paper highlights. Confident contour lines over the hatching. The panel is composed full, corner to corner, and rewards a second look. Black-and-white only; no flat fills, no cel shading, no photographic rendering, no color.

THE ROOM. Inside The Swinging Door: upscale, current, a block off Wall Street, never a dive; polished MARBLE bar top, fine walnut-paneled walls, leather armchairs and studded club chairs. ONE LARGE MODERN WINDOW fills the street wall at frame-left — a single tall sheet of clear plate glass, NO small panes, NO muntin bars, NO frosting. Through it, PRESENT-DAY NEW YORK CITY at bar height: building faces, glass-and-steel over older stone, daylight — the view begins ABOVE the street floor, so NO pavement, NO roadway, NO sidewalk, NO bollards and NO people are visible through the glass. The bar's name is mirrored on the glass as read from inside, SPELLED LETTER BY LETTER — T-H-E S-W-I-N-G-I-N-G D-O-O-R, both G's present; nothing else is lettered on or beyond the glass. Back bar of distinct bottle shapes, the SAME collection every day, and the bottles are VISIBLY FILLED TO DIFFERENT LEVELS — some near full, some half, a few low; a row of identical empties is a redraw. EVERY BOTTLE WEARS A PLAIN LABEL WITH NO WORDS ON IT: panels of varied shape — tall, oval, banded, some striped — and NOT ONE carries a letter, number or mark that looks like writing; a lettered bottle is a redraw. Beside the bottles, CLEAN GLASSWARE: a neat row of polished rocks glasses and coupes, stemware hanging above, never cluttered. On the FAR SERVICE SIDE toward frame-right, a compact TAP TOWER — three or four classy beer taps, polished brass and turned-wood handles, NO lettering, badge or logo on any handle — never hiding a face, never on the gentlemen's side. Shelving: SERVICE side, never behind the gentlemen; on their side a bottle appears ONLY in Abby's hand or set down by her. THE ONLY CHARACTERS IN THE ROOM ARE THIS CARTOON'S CAST; Abby the ONLY bartender. NO other figures anywhere in the bar, OF ANY SPECIES: no other customers, no staff, none in the mirror; no second dog or bird invented to fill a gap — the room behind the cast is furniture, bottles, panelling and signage only. Single exception: the TELEVISION SCREEN, where broadcast footage may show people. Covers pictures as well as people: no human figure in the room, picture frame or hat included; framed prints on the panelling and any emblem on clothing are NON-FIGURATIVE: architecture, landscape, animals, still life, a ship, a bull, a bottle. On the CAST no emblem at all: no badge, crest, monogram, logo or device on cap, visor, polo, vest, jacket. Barclay's flag pin is the ONLY thing worn on anyone's clothing in this strip.

The TV and the chalkboard are OPTIONAL, shown only when they serve THIS cartoon and only on its subject. THE TELEVISION'S FRAME AND SURROUND ARE BARE BLACK PLASTIC WITH NOTHING WRITTEN ON THEM ANYWHERE — no brand, badge, plate or bezel glyphs. IT IS A TELEVISION AND IT IS SWITCHED ON — a LARGE wall-mounted flatscreen, the WIDEST single thing on the back wall, spanning the back bar's central bay in a narrow black bezel, showing live footage, never a framed print or notice. No CNBC bug and no chyron band means it is not a television, and the panel is wrong. The flatscreen over the back bar carries full broadcast grammar: CNBC network bug with LIVE tag, bold-caps headline chyron on a lower-third band, time stamp at right edge. NO SECOND LINE OF TEXT ON THE SCREEN — no ticker, no crawl, no strapline; the chyron carries every word the screen says and reads TEN OF ELEVEN S&P SECTORS FALL TO OPEN SEPTEMBER. THE PICTURE ILLUSTRATES THAT VERY HEADLINE: invent the footage this story would actually show, in the same engraved style. Never repeat a picture from a reference image. COUNT THE WORDS INSIDE THE TELEVISION PICTURE: ZERO. The footage itself carries NO lettering anywhere — not on a sign, a shopfront, a licence plate, a carton, a label, a receipt, a chart axis, a screen or a vehicle; where the scene would carry writing, DRAW THAT SURFACE BLANK. A chalkboard carries menu-shaped jokes in hand-lettered chalk serifs reading exactly and only: REGULAR, FRIDAY $61 / REGULAR, TUESDAY $74 / PAY AT THE PUMP. THE BOARD PRICES THE JOKE — it NEVER urges drinking hard, fast or often. AND THE WHOLE BOARD IS IN THE PICTURE: its dark wooden frame visible on ALL FOUR SIDES, never cropped by the panel's edge — a board half out of frame is a redraw. All lettering is REAL, correctly spelled English, cleanly drawn, easily readable at a glance — never scribbled, garbled, invented filler, repeated words, or lettering the scene did not ask for. THERE IS A SIZE BELOW WHICH NOTHING IS LETTERED AT ALL: if a word would be drawn smaller than the height of a character's eye, IT IS NOT DRAWN — that surface is completely blank, plain and unmarked. It governs every small object — club faces, watch dials, bottle caps. Marks that merely LOOK like writing come back as broken glyphs: a blank club face is correct, a scribbled one a redraw. A PRINTED PROP — bill, receipt, folio, menu, boarding pass — CARRIES AT MOST FOUR LINES OF TEXT, each large enough to read at a glance, named by this brief; the rest is BLANK WHITE. There is no fine print in this strip: a receipt with rows of illegible marks is a redraw. AND NOTHING PRINTED LIES ON THE MARBLE: no note card, no slip, no loose receipt, no card reader on the bar top — a printed prop appears ONLY when this brief names one, and then it is held UP IN A HAND, large enough to read. AND NOTHING IS TAGGED: no price tag, sticker or ticket hangs from any glass, bottle or held object. Shared nut bowl, napkins, coasters on the marble.

THE STAGE. The staging is physically real. A bar scene is CROPPED AT THE COUNTER: the picture ends at the marble or the panelling just below it, exactly as the plates crop it. Nothing below the counter is ever in frame: no legs, no knees, no thighs, no feet, no shoes, no stool seats, no stool legs, no footrests, no floor. The two gentlemen: close in, roughly the chest up, composed exactly as the reference plates; Abby, when cast, is set BACK beyond the slab. Every face: THREE-QUARTER view, angled into frame so face and both eyes are fully visible — the gentlemen are SEEN FROM BEHIND from the customer side, yet each face turns into frame; never a full back of a head, never a head cranked round to face the camera. COUNT THE EYES. BARCLAY AND ABBY have BOTH EYES DRAWN ON THE PAPER, the FAR eye AT LEAST HALF THE WIDTH of the near one, bridge of muzzle showing between them — their faces are broad and carry the turn, and one eye hidden behind the muzzle is a redraw on either. THE FIX IS IN THE SEATING, NOT THE NECK: turn the body further round on its chair until the far eye reappears. DREW IS THE EXCEPTION AND HE KEEPS HIS PROFILE. A flamingo's skull is narrow and his bill is long, so a three-quarter view crowds the bill across his face; he may show ONE eye, and it is the MOST FULLY MODELLED THING ON HIS HEAD — a clear round iris, a distinct pupil, one catchlight, a defined upper lid with a crease and a soft lower lid, never a flat bead. His head still turns toward whoever he is with. NOBODY LOOKS OUT OF THE PANEL AT THE READER. Every gaze stays in the scene. A figure staring straight down the lens is a redraw. BARCLAY HAS ABSOLUTELY NO TAIL. No caption, dialogue line, speech balloon or typeset band is ever drawn above or below the art: the panel is the drawing only, the house sets words afterwards. NOBODY IS WEARING THEIR OWN SKIN: feathers and fur GROW OUT OF them, never drawn as a garment — no cuff, hem, seam, shoulder line, lapel edge or closing line anywhere in plumage or coat, and a second line crossing Drew's arm below his vest's armhole reads as a jacket sleeve and the panel is wrong. Never a wingtip or a fan of long primaries for a hand: long wing feathers belong on Drew's BACK and SIDES, end at his hip, never run down the arm. On Barclay's coat and Abby's clothes fur meets cloth at the garment's own edge, nowhere else.

THE HOUSE NAME IS BUILT INTO THE OBJECT, NEVER ONTO THE CAST. Objects carry THE SWINGING DOOR the way a real maker would put it there: EMBOSSED or blind-stamped into leather, WOVEN into a napkin's weave, PRESSED into glass or porcelain, FOIL-STAMPED on a folder, BURNED into wood, ETCHED into metal. It is made of the object's own material and takes the object's own light, curve and wear — a mark you could feel with a thumb, following the surface as the surface bends, sitting where a maker would sign, in the house's engraved script, small and neat and sized to the object. THE TEST: if removing it would leave the object looking untouched then it was printed ON and it is wrong. Never a sticker, decal, patch, tag, badge or floating label lying on top. COUNT IT BEFORE YOU FINISH: find the ONE object in this panel that most obviously belongs to the cast or the house — the golf bag, the bill folder, the tote, the tray — and put the mark on THAT ONE first, before any other lettering in the picture, even when it stands in the background and even when it already carries a joke of its own, the two marks sitting apart. A panel that HAS such an object and leaves it unmarked is unfinished; a panel with NO cast-owned object needs no mark, and never add a prop just to carry the name. ABBY'S BAR TOWEL IS THE ONE EXCEPTION AND CARRIES NOTHING, EVER: plain white cloth, no name, no monogram, no woven mark, no lettering of any kind — a marked bar towel is a redraw.

THE BAR IS ONE LEVEL. COUNT THE HORIZONTAL MARBLE SURFACES: EXACTLY ONE — a single continuous flat slab of pale grey veined MARBLE at one height across the picture, walnut edge below. A second marble surface at ANY other height is a redraw. AND IT IS ONE STRAIGHT PLANE: where the marble shows beside a gentleman it lines up EXACTLY with the marble in front of him — one LEVEL top edge, parallel to the picture's bottom, frame-left to frame-right, never receding toward the window; a slab that steps up or tilts is a redraw. The back bar carries its bottles on HIGH SHELVES ONLY — the lowest shelf sits above the standing bartender's shoulders, plain fielded walnut panelling below.

THE SEATING IS THE SAME EVERY DAY: studded oxblood leather club chairs with brass nailheads along their backs. At most the top of a chair back shows behind each gentleman's own back at the frame's edge — never a seat, never a stool leg.

THE BAR HEIGHT IS FIXED, AND IT IS A TALL BAR — a real 42-inch counter, its top level with a seated man's mid-chest, never as low as his waist or belt. THE SLAB IS A SURFACE BEYOND HIM, NEVER A BAND DRAWN ACROSS HIM: no part of it overlaps, cuts across or passes through a gentleman's chest, waist, vest or jacket — his whole torso stands IN FRONT of the near edge and hides it, and only his forearms and his drink reach onto the top. A man with marble drawn across his body sits half sunk into the bar, and that is a redraw.

THE SIDES — absolute, and the thing this strip gets wrong most often. THE PROHIBITIONS FIRST: EXACTLY ONE counter, never a second counter, table, back ledge or work-top and never a nearer surface invented for the drinks; and the BACK BAR — bottles, mirror, television, chalkboard — stands ACROSS THE COUNTER on the FAR SERVICE SIDE with an EMPTY WALKWAY between the slab's far edge and its shelves — the shelves NEVER rise from the counter's edge and NEVER behind a gentleman's head. THE CAMERA is on the CUSTOMER SIDE, just behind and above the two gentlemen, looking ACROSS the one counter — one long slab of marble running LEFT TO RIGHT out of frame at both ends, never a wedge, never an island — to that back bar. DREW AND BARCLAY SIT AT ITS NEAR SIDE, close and large, SEEN FROM BEHIND and TURNED TOWARD EACH OTHER so each face reads in THREE-QUARTER over his own shoulder. THE GENTLEMEN ARE BETWEEN THE CAMERA AND THE COUNTER: each man's body BLOCKS the slab's near edge where he sits, so the marble shows only BETWEEN and BESIDE them at chest height — NEVER as an unbroken strip crossing in front of their chests. A gentleman the counter passes IN FRONT OF is standing in the bartender's place, and that is a redraw. AND WHEN ABBY IS NOT NAMED, THE FAR SERVICE SIDE HOLDS NO ONE — no bartender, no server, no second dog, no figure polishing a glass. COUNT THE FIGURES BEFORE YOU DRAW ANY OF THEM: this panel contains the characters this brief names and NOBODY ELSE, and inventing someone on the service side is a redraw.

NEAREST THE READER, DREW AND BARCLAY, SEATED AT THE COUNTER AND TURNED TOWARD EACH OTHER, seen FROM BEHIND from the customer side: Drew frame-LEFT, Barclay frame-RIGHT, each body turned only a quarter toward the other so the reader catches his face in THREE-QUARTER over his own shoulder. His own back and hip COVER the counter's near edge where he sits; the marble reaches the camera only beside and between the two of them, and the back bar stands far ACROSS it — never at his back. The BODY does the turning, so Barclay's far eye lands on the paper with no crank in his neck; Drew keeps his one-eyed profile, his head turned toward Barclay so the bill angles ACROSS the picture. Each man's chest still angles toward the marble, both forearms resting ON it and his drink on the slab in front of him, chest and shoulders rising CLEAR ABOVE its near edge. Nobody sits or perches ON the slab, and nobody hangs back from the bar he is drinking at.

NEXT, THE MARBLE COUNTER ITSELF, carrying Drew's martini, Barclay's old fashioned and the shared nut bowl side by side on its one surface, between and before the gentlemen where their hands can reach. THE COUNTER IS NEVER A STRIP ALONG THE BOTTOM OF THE FRAME WITH ALL THREE FIGURES BEHIND IT — that is what makes the gentlemen read as bartenders — and it is NEVER a table, a booth, a desk or a ledge: it is the bar's own slab, and the gentlemen are its patrons.

FARTHEST, PAST THE COUNTER, THE SERVICE SIDE: first the counter's FAR EDGE drawn as its own clean marble line beyond the drinks, then the walkway, then the back bar with its bottles and mirror, the television above it, the chalkboard beside — and ABBY when she is named, facing them, THE COUNTER'S FAR EDGE CROSSING HER AT THE WAIST and hiding her below it; she stands and they sit, so HER HEAD SITS HIGHER IN THE FRAME THAN THEIRS.

The two of them are on one side and she is on the other, always, and they never swap. When it is ambiguous the prop settles it: ANY LIQUOR BOTTLE OR BAR TOWEL IN THE PANEL IS ABBY'S — in her hands or on her shoulder — never in theirs. A stemmed glass has exactly ONE bowl on ONE stem on ONE foot — never a doubled stem, never two feet, never a second outline behind the hand. Every prop rests ON the marble or in a closed grip — nothing floats, nothing merges or clips. A LIFTED GLASS LEAVES ITS NAPKIN AND COASTER FLAT ON THE MARBLE: nothing sticks to the foot of a raised glass.

DREW. Preserve Drew exactly as the reference plates draw him (canon/vision/drew-plate1-bar-reference.jpg is the definitive study — the bar Drew of plate 1, with the LONG graceful high S-curve neck and the SMALL refined head; never a short thick neck, never a hunched or heavy bird. HIS BILL IS SLENDER, AND THE BLACK IS A MARKING ON IT RATHER THAN A PART OF IT. Two rules decide the shape, and they are the two the drawing keeps getting wrong.

FIRST, DEPTH. The bill is SLENDER: where it meets the feathers, its depth top-to-bottom is about ONE THIRD of its length. It tapers from there to the tip. Take the shape from a SWAN: a slender bill of even taper, bending in one gentle unbroken curve, with a small dark patch at the very tip. Its length is not the problem — a long slender bill is right; a thick one is wrong.

HIS BILL IS SLENDER AND IT DOES NOT BREAK. It leaves the face tucked and close, drops STEEPLY and STRAIGHT, and continues its own single curve smoothly to a ROUNDED TIP — one unbroken line from base to tip with no angle, no elbow, no kink and no hook anywhere along it. LAY A RULER ALONG THE UNDERSIDE AND IT SHOULD TOUCH ALMOST THE WHOLE LENGTH. The tip never hangs below the line the bill was already travelling on, and it never widens into a deep spoon. The rear two thirds are PALE; along the OUTER THIRD ONLY, the black IS the outline — it continues the bill's own curve rather than swelling into a bulb — with one bright highlight ribbon inside it. The NOSTRIL is a plain thin slit about HALF the length of his eye, with NO ring, outline or fleshy surround around it. There is no shelf or ridge above the eye.

He is FAR MORE FLAMINGO THAN HUMAN — plump, soft-bodied and FEATHERED ALL OVER in fine dash-strokes: breast, shoulders, back and arms, with long scalloped wing-feathers beneath each forearm. No human skin, torso, musculature or face anywhere; he is a bird who happens to sit at a bar. His neck is thick at the shoulders and rises in the deep question-mark sweep of a true flamingo, turning over at the top so the head hangs forward of where the neck left the body. His eyes are heavy-lidded and deadpan — visible white, distinct dark iris and pupil, a drooping upper lid and one fine contour line above it — never a bird dot. His face is AMIABLE: plump, softly modelled cheeks and a faint smile-line, a man who has heard it before and is fond of you anyway; never gaunt, hollow-eyed, sunken or sinister.

NO HAND IN THIS PANEL HAS A NAIL ON IT. Not Drew's, not Barclay's, not Abby's: every fingertip in the picture ends BLUNT AND SOFT in fur, plumage or pad, and a drawn nail, claw, talon or crescent at any fingertip is a redraw wherever it appears. THE ONLY HUMANLIKE THING ABOUT HIM IS HIS HANDS. Each feathered arm ends in a genuine hand — four slender fingers and an opposed thumb, feather-covered to the tips, elegant on a martini stem. WHITE PLUMAGE RUNS UNBROKEN FROM SHOULDER TO FINGERTIP: no sleeve, no cuff, no hem, no seam anywhere on the arm, and nothing smooth or bare-skinned anywhere on him. A crisp starched WHITE collar band circles the base of his neck and his small solid-black silk bow tie sits at the throat in front of it. DRAW THE TIE AS A TIED BOW: TWO wings of equal size spreading left and right, each wider at its outer edge, pinched to a SMALL CENTRE KNOT; horizontal, level, centred under the chin, resting ON the collar. Never one lump, never tilted, never more than two wings. THE BOW IS THE ONLY BLACK AT HIS NECK — no band, ribbon, strap, cord or choker runs around it or behind the bow. He wears a V-neck knitted sweater vest in fine honeycomb stitch with ribbed edges over a pale collared shirt, and trousers; THE VEST IS PLAIN KNIT WITH NO POCKETS ANYWHERE — none on the front, and never a pocket, flap or panel on the back. His plumage is pale but hatched — fine dash-strokes over white, high midtone rather than bare paper. At the bar his martini is always within reach: conical stemmed glass, ONE olive on ONE pick, on a napkin or coaster, held by the stem when lifted. His seat is frame-left, neck arched so his face hangs where the gag needs it. WHEN THIS SCENE HAS DREW SPEAKING his bill is SLIGHTLY PARTED, caught mid-word — never a clamped-shut bill on the one who is talking. At golf he adds a visor; a monocle is an approved occasional accessory.

BARCLAY. A successful gentleman in his mid-forties, unmistakably a golden retriever, drawn like one (canon/vision/barclay-reference.jpg is the definitive study): fur layered in fine individual strokes, drop ears with long fringe, broad soft-eyed retriever face, freckled muzzle, true black dog lips, dark lip-line along the muzzle from under his black nose, chest ruff modest, never a heavy neck-beard; middle-aged, solid, rounded shoulders, modest belly, absolutely no tail. HIS MOUTH IS CLOSED IN EVERY PANEL — never hanging open, never panting, never a visible tongue, never bared teeth. Default read: worried, earnest everyman against Drew's deadpan — BUT HE IS NOT SAD, and the first glance must not read as sad. Worry in the BROWS ONLY: raised inner brows, faint forehead wrinkle. Below the brows all WARM: mouth corners gently UP into a soft closed-lip smile, eyes bright and open, a clear catchlight in each, cheeks full and lifted. Read: a good-humoured man a little concerned, never a downcast one: mouth up, brows up, eyes bright. Hands visibly a dog's: broad, fur-backed, soft-padded fingers, NO NAILS OR CLAWS DRAWN AT ALL, each fingertip ending in soft fur and pad, never in a nail, yet fully humanoid in articulation: four fingers and an opposed thumb, believable human grips. At the bar, his dark suit jacket over a pale open-collared shirt, no tie; for daytime, travel, golf, a pale collared polo, dark leather belt, (outdoors) a ball cap; at golf his bag stands at frame-right, towel on its front hand-lettered in three lines FORE! / NOT SO / FAST. The small USA flag pin is PERMANENT: left lapel when jacketed, left chest of shirt or polo otherwise; on whatever he wears. A wristwatch on his left wrist in every panel EXCEPT at golf: a white golf glove on his left hand takes its place on that same wrist, smooth, unfurred to the cuff, forearm above it still furred; the watch and the glove are never both drawn, never on opposite sides of him. IN A BAR PANEL his old fashioned (short rocks glass, one large cube, one dark cherry) rests flat at frame-right, the shared bowl of bar nuts between the two drinks; AWAY FROM THE BAR he brings neither, whatever he holds belongs to the place he is in.

Drew and Barclay are gentlemen — classy, composed, well turned out; all three principals carry wisdom and command respect purely by how they carry themselves. Nothing about them is ever crude, sloppy or loud, and every scene carries that high-class read. Text inside the panel lives ON things and is a gag layer: whatever lettered surfaces THIS setting actually has — a chyron, a menu or scoreboard, a posted notice, a banner, a placard, a label — may each carry a short, legible, hand-lettered joke DRAWN FROM THE SAME JOKE as the caption, so the place and the line land as one gag from several angles. Letter ONLY the surfaces this setting genuinely has. No speech balloons, no thought bubbles, and no floating caption text inside the art — the dialogue is typeset by the house beneath the panel. THE SCENE: Barclay, earnest and resigned, swirls the ice in his old fashioned; Drew, deadpan, studies him over the rim of his martini; Abby, laughing, tops up the nut bowl in front of Barclay with a generous shake. IN THIS PANEL, CAMERA behind the two gentlemen on the CUSTOMER SIDE — their bodies block the counter's near edge — with ABBY working the FAR service side across the counter, the back bar behind HER alone. The television picture shows A gas pump with its nozzle hung in the cradle, the price display blank. Stage it exactly as THE SIDES describes. Abby is SMILING in this panel — an unmistakable smile, mouth corners up, eyes bright — NEVER sad, neutral or downcast; her beat is ACTIVE and cheerful: pouring, presenting a glass, laughing at her own line.

ABBY. Abby is the successful proprietor of The Swinging Door — a glamorous, feminine West Highland White Terrier in her mid-forties who owns the room and works its bar, drawn in the same engraved technique (canon/vision/abby-face-reference.jpg is the definitive face study): a true fluffy westie face in fine individual fur strokes, the head taken from a GROOMED SHOW WESTIE. HER FACE IS EXACTLY THE FACE OF HER STUDY, and wherever these words and that picture differ, THE PICTURE WINS. It is a small fluffy show-groomed head, ROUND AND SOFT: her big black nose sits DIRECTLY UNDER HER EYES on a round fluffy face — there is NO projecting muzzle to draw at all, no bridge, no cone, NO snout ever; nose, eyes and tiny closed smile all live on the front of one soft round head, and nothing sharp, foxish or wolfish appears anywhere. Her face reads SOFT, PRETTY, WARM and unmistakably FEMININE: long lashes, groomed brows, the fluff around her face shaped the way a stylist would leave it. HER EYES ARE HER BEST FEATURE AND THE MOST BEAUTIFUL THING IN THE PANEL. THEY ARE GLAMOROUS, LIDDED EYES, not a puppy's buttons: the upper lid sits low and sultry over the iris, the dark lash line is HEAVY and sweeps up and out at the corner, a bright catchlight sits high in each, and her look is warm, knowing and sidelong. Each is built like a HUMAN eye: a wide almond, WIDER THAN IT IS TALL, tilted up at the outer corner, white showing both sides of a drawn IRIS with a smaller round PUPIL. Draw them LARGE — EACH EYE AT LEAST AS WIDE AS THE BLACK OF HER NOSE — clear, bright and alert. Two or three fine brow strokes above each, two small pricked ears, and A SMILE IN EVERY PANEL — an unmistakable smile, mouth corners clearly UP and eyes bright, closed-lip or a happy open smile, whether she is at rest, serving or landing a line; a straight, neutral, pursed or downcast mouth on her is a redraw, as are drooping brows or mournful eyes. She is turned into the frame only as far as keeps BOTH EYES ON THE PAPER, the far eye at least half the width of the near one, the bridge of her muzzle showing between them. Her body is slightly humanoid, built exactly like the two gentlemen: upright on two legs, humanoid shoulders and arms, and fur-backed dog-yet-humanoid hands with soft pads and FOUR FINGERS AND AN OPPOSED THUMB, every finger separately drawn, closing on glass, towel and bottle neck in believable human grips. Trim, natural and graceful: a clean shoulder line and a waist the reader can find. HER FIGURE IS SLIM AND HER BUST IS SMALL AND NATURAL — the placket of her blouse runs very nearly STRAIGHT DOWN her front and the front reads as one gentle plane, never two separated volumes with a shadowed cleft between them. Her blouse is UNBUTTONED TWO BUTTONS DOWN so the collar falls open in a soft V, and the V falls open DEEP ENOUGH THAT THE SMOOTH CURVE OF HER CLEAVAGE SHOWS, drawn frankly attractive: throat, collarbone and the soft shadowed line between the curves, all reading as smooth skin. THE FUR IS WHAT SPOILS IT, so the long fur of her head and cheeks STOPS at her jawline and below it everything is SHORT, FINE and CLOSE-LYING — not one ruff, tuft or wisp of fluff breaks the clean line of the V. It is a LOWER NECKLINE, never a larger bust, and a shaggy chest inside an open collar is a redraw. She wears her fitted light blouse with rolled sleeves, a dark fitted skirt, a studded leather collar with a small teardrop gem pendant at its centre, a pearl bracelet and black heels; absolutely no tail. Her folded bar towel is ALWAYS SOMEWHERE IN THE PANEL, never missing from it, and in EXACTLY ONE PLACE AND NEVER BOTH: either draped over her LEFT SHOULDER with both hands empty of it, or held in her hands round the glass she is polishing with her shoulder BARE. There is only one towel in the panel. IN A BAR PANEL she works the service side directly across the marble from the gentlemen, standing to it on her own two feet with her arms free, visibly mid-task with ONE HAND CLOSED ON A WORKING OBJECT — glass, bottle, towel, chalk, or whatever THIS scene hands her; when the scene gives her its own object to handle, the towel rides her LEFT SHOULDER and both hands stay free of it — and the panel crops at the counter, its far edge cutting her at the waist and hiding her below it. AWAY FROM THE BAR she stands on the ground like everyone else, there on a named errand of the house, still with her towel and still with one hand busy, with no counter to stand behind, and the panel crops at whatever edge that setting names.

title: energy was today s only winner (r1b-1-raw.png)
caption: Energy was today's only winner, and I'm short it through the Suburban.
tv: TEN OF ELEVEN S&P SECTORS FALL TO OPEN SEPTEMBER
board: REGULAR, FRIDAY $61 / REGULAR, TUESDAY $74 / PAY AT THE PUMP
prompt:
Draw ONE single-panel black-and-white gag cartoon, one unbroken scene edge to edge — no seam, no split, no second frame, and no photographic rendering.

REFERENCES. @image1 is Drew, exactly as the studio's official portrait — copy THIS bird identically: the bill, the black bow tie, the knitted sweater vest, and the feathered hands with four fingers and a thumb and no claws. The cartoon's Drew must be indistinguishable from this one. @image2 is Barclay, exactly as the studio's official portrait — copy THIS dog identically: both eyes on the paper, the closed mouth, the flag pin on his left lapel, the wristwatch, the fur-backed clawless hands. The cartoon's Barclay must be indistinguishable from this one. @image3 is Abby, exactly as the studio's official portrait — copy THIS lady identically: the round soft head with the big black nose close under the eyes and no muzzle, the glamorous lidded eyes, the smooth open neckline, the studded collar with its gem, the towel. The cartoon's Abby must be indistinguishable from this one. @image4 is a FINISHED PANEL of this exact strip: the SAME room, the SAME cast in the SAME seats, poses and expressions, the same drinks on the same counter, the same window and shelves. COPY IT LINE FOR LINE — and change ONLY what the scene below orders: the television's picture and headline and the chalkboard's lettering, plus any detail this description names differently from the tile (bottle labels, taps, glassware, a smile). If this scene casts a character the tile does not show — Abby, on the FAR service side across the counter — ADD her exactly as described below without moving or redrawing anyone the tile already has. HER FACE IS THE FACE OF HER OWN PORTRAIT TILE, NOT INVENTED: a round, soft, fluffy show-westie head with NO muzzle or snout, big glamorous lidded eyes, a small black nose right under them, and a wide happy smile — nothing narrow, sharp, foxish or wolfish; a pointed face or a thin mouth on her is a redraw. Everything else stays exactly as the tile draws it, including the counter's panelled front face at frame-left. THE TELEVISION KEEPS ITS BROADCAST GRAMMAR exactly as the tile shows it — the CNBC LIVE bug, the ONE-LINE headline band across the bottom of the screen reading this scene's headline, and the time stamp; a screen showing only a picture with no headline band is a redraw. THE COUNTER'S TOP EDGE RUNS LEVEL across the picture — parallel to the bottom edge, the same height at Drew's window end as in front of him, never receding upward toward the window. FRAME THE ROOM EXACTLY AS THE TILE FRAMES IT: the television high on the wall with the whole chalkboard beside it, the marble counter with every glass and the nut bowl in the LOWER THIRD of the picture, and the TOPS OF BOTH STUDDED LEATHER CHAIR BACKS showing along the bottom edge, exactly as in the tile. Your canvas is taller than the tile: the BOTTOM SIXTH of your canvas will be trimmed away, so put nothing that matters there — only the lower parts of the two chair backs — and keep the counter, the drinks and the chair-back tops ABOVE that band. Draw each character exactly as his or her own reference draws that character — same face, same build, same wardrobe — and give the panel the same antique-engraving hand. Do NOT reproduce any reference's own background, signage, lettering, or composition: every word of lettering in this cartoon comes from the scene described below, and nothing else.

The finished panel contains EXACTLY 3 characters, each a separate individual — never merged, never duplicated, never omitted.

THE CARTOON:

A single-panel gag cartoon drawn like an antique steel engraving: fine pen crosshatching and stippling on every surface — wood grain, knit stitches, fur and feathers laid in individual strokes, glass catching light — with a full tonal range from deep rich blacks through silvery greys to bright paper highlights. Confident contour lines over the hatching. The panel is composed full, corner to corner, and rewards a second look. Black-and-white only; no flat fills, no cel shading, no photographic rendering, no color.

THE ROOM. Inside The Swinging Door: upscale, current, a block off Wall Street, never a dive; polished MARBLE bar top, fine walnut-paneled walls, leather armchairs and studded club chairs. ONE LARGE MODERN WINDOW fills the street wall at frame-left — a single tall sheet of clear plate glass, NO small panes, NO muntin bars, NO frosting. Through it, PRESENT-DAY NEW YORK CITY at bar height: building faces, glass-and-steel over older stone, daylight — the view begins ABOVE the street floor, so NO pavement, NO roadway, NO sidewalk, NO bollards and NO people are visible through the glass. The bar's name is mirrored on the glass as read from inside, SPELLED LETTER BY LETTER — T-H-E S-W-I-N-G-I-N-G D-O-O-R, both G's present; nothing else is lettered on or beyond the glass. Back bar of distinct bottle shapes, the SAME collection every day, and the bottles are VISIBLY FILLED TO DIFFERENT LEVELS — some near full, some half, a few low; a row of identical empties is a redraw. EVERY BOTTLE WEARS A PLAIN LABEL WITH NO WORDS ON IT: panels of varied shape — tall, oval, banded, some striped — and NOT ONE carries a letter, number or mark that looks like writing; a lettered bottle is a redraw. Beside the bottles, CLEAN GLASSWARE: a neat row of polished rocks glasses and coupes, stemware hanging above, never cluttered. On the FAR SERVICE SIDE toward frame-right, a compact TAP TOWER — three or four classy beer taps, polished brass and turned-wood handles, NO lettering, badge or logo on any handle — never hiding a face, never on the gentlemen's side. Shelving: SERVICE side, never behind the gentlemen; on their side a bottle appears ONLY in Abby's hand or set down by her. THE ONLY CHARACTERS IN THE ROOM ARE THIS CARTOON'S CAST; Abby the ONLY bartender. NO other figures anywhere in the bar, OF ANY SPECIES: no other customers, no staff, none in the mirror; no second dog or bird invented to fill a gap — the room behind the cast is furniture, bottles, panelling and signage only. Single exception: the TELEVISION SCREEN, where broadcast footage may show people. Covers pictures as well as people: no human figure in the room, picture frame or hat included; framed prints on the panelling and any emblem on clothing are NON-FIGURATIVE: architecture, landscape, animals, still life, a ship, a bull, a bottle. On the CAST no emblem at all: no badge, crest, monogram, logo or device on cap, visor, polo, vest, jacket. Barclay's flag pin is the ONLY thing worn on anyone's clothing in this strip.

The TV and the chalkboard are OPTIONAL, shown only when they serve THIS cartoon and only on its subject. THE TELEVISION'S FRAME AND SURROUND ARE BARE BLACK PLASTIC WITH NOTHING WRITTEN ON THEM ANYWHERE — no brand, badge, plate or bezel glyphs. IT IS A TELEVISION AND IT IS SWITCHED ON — a LARGE wall-mounted flatscreen, the WIDEST single thing on the back wall, spanning the back bar's central bay in a narrow black bezel, showing live footage, never a framed print or notice. No CNBC bug and no chyron band means it is not a television, and the panel is wrong. The flatscreen over the back bar carries full broadcast grammar: CNBC network bug with LIVE tag, bold-caps headline chyron on a lower-third band, time stamp at right edge. NO SECOND LINE OF TEXT ON THE SCREEN — no ticker, no crawl, no strapline; the chyron carries every word the screen says and reads TEN OF ELEVEN S&P SECTORS FALL TO OPEN SEPTEMBER. THE PICTURE ILLUSTRATES THAT VERY HEADLINE: invent the footage this story would actually show, in the same engraved style. Never repeat a picture from a reference image. COUNT THE WORDS INSIDE THE TELEVISION PICTURE: ZERO. The footage itself carries NO lettering anywhere — not on a sign, a shopfront, a licence plate, a carton, a label, a receipt, a chart axis, a screen or a vehicle; where the scene would carry writing, DRAW THAT SURFACE BLANK. A chalkboard carries menu-shaped jokes in hand-lettered chalk serifs reading exactly and only: REGULAR, FRIDAY $61 / REGULAR, TUESDAY $74 / PAY AT THE PUMP. THE BOARD PRICES THE JOKE — it NEVER urges drinking hard, fast or often. AND THE WHOLE BOARD IS IN THE PICTURE: its dark wooden frame visible on ALL FOUR SIDES, never cropped by the panel's edge — a board half out of frame is a redraw. All lettering is REAL, correctly spelled English, cleanly drawn, easily readable at a glance — never scribbled, garbled, invented filler, repeated words, or lettering the scene did not ask for. THERE IS A SIZE BELOW WHICH NOTHING IS LETTERED AT ALL: if a word would be drawn smaller than the height of a character's eye, IT IS NOT DRAWN — that surface is completely blank, plain and unmarked. It governs every small object — club faces, watch dials, bottle caps. Marks that merely LOOK like writing come back as broken glyphs: a blank club face is correct, a scribbled one a redraw. A PRINTED PROP — bill, receipt, folio, menu, boarding pass — CARRIES AT MOST FOUR LINES OF TEXT, each large enough to read at a glance, named by this brief; the rest is BLANK WHITE. There is no fine print in this strip: a receipt with rows of illegible marks is a redraw. AND NOTHING PRINTED LIES ON THE MARBLE: no note card, no slip, no loose receipt, no card reader on the bar top — a printed prop appears ONLY when this brief names one, and then it is held UP IN A HAND, large enough to read. AND NOTHING IS TAGGED: no price tag, sticker or ticket hangs from any glass, bottle or held object. Shared nut bowl, napkins, coasters on the marble.

THE STAGE. The staging is physically real. A bar scene is CROPPED AT THE COUNTER: the picture ends at the marble or the panelling just below it, exactly as the plates crop it. Nothing below the counter is ever in frame: no legs, no knees, no thighs, no feet, no shoes, no stool seats, no stool legs, no footrests, no floor. The two gentlemen: close in, roughly the chest up, composed exactly as the reference plates; Abby, when cast, is set BACK beyond the slab. Every face: THREE-QUARTER view, angled into frame so face and both eyes are fully visible — the gentlemen are SEEN FROM BEHIND from the customer side, yet each face turns into frame; never a full back of a head, never a head cranked round to face the camera. COUNT THE EYES. BARCLAY AND ABBY have BOTH EYES DRAWN ON THE PAPER, the FAR eye AT LEAST HALF THE WIDTH of the near one, bridge of muzzle showing between them — their faces are broad and carry the turn, and one eye hidden behind the muzzle is a redraw on either. THE FIX IS IN THE SEATING, NOT THE NECK: turn the body further round on its chair until the far eye reappears. DREW IS THE EXCEPTION AND HE KEEPS HIS PROFILE. A flamingo's skull is narrow and his bill is long, so a three-quarter view crowds the bill across his face; he may show ONE eye, and it is the MOST FULLY MODELLED THING ON HIS HEAD — a clear round iris, a distinct pupil, one catchlight, a defined upper lid with a crease and a soft lower lid, never a flat bead. His head still turns toward whoever he is with. NOBODY LOOKS OUT OF THE PANEL AT THE READER. Every gaze stays in the scene. A figure staring straight down the lens is a redraw. BARCLAY HAS ABSOLUTELY NO TAIL. No caption, dialogue line, speech balloon or typeset band is ever drawn above or below the art: the panel is the drawing only, the house sets words afterwards. NOBODY IS WEARING THEIR OWN SKIN: feathers and fur GROW OUT OF them, never drawn as a garment — no cuff, hem, seam, shoulder line, lapel edge or closing line anywhere in plumage or coat, and a second line crossing Drew's arm below his vest's armhole reads as a jacket sleeve and the panel is wrong. Never a wingtip or a fan of long primaries for a hand: long wing feathers belong on Drew's BACK and SIDES, end at his hip, never run down the arm. On Barclay's coat and Abby's clothes fur meets cloth at the garment's own edge, nowhere else.

THE HOUSE NAME IS BUILT INTO THE OBJECT, NEVER ONTO THE CAST. Objects carry THE SWINGING DOOR the way a real maker would put it there: EMBOSSED or blind-stamped into leather, WOVEN into a napkin's weave, PRESSED into glass or porcelain, FOIL-STAMPED on a folder, BURNED into wood, ETCHED into metal. It is made of the object's own material and takes the object's own light, curve and wear — a mark you could feel with a thumb, following the surface as the surface bends, sitting where a maker would sign, in the house's engraved script, small and neat and sized to the object. THE TEST: if removing it would leave the object looking untouched then it was printed ON and it is wrong. Never a sticker, decal, patch, tag, badge or floating label lying on top. COUNT IT BEFORE YOU FINISH: find the ONE object in this panel that most obviously belongs to the cast or the house — the golf bag, the bill folder, the tote, the tray — and put the mark on THAT ONE first, before any other lettering in the picture, even when it stands in the background and even when it already carries a joke of its own, the two marks sitting apart. A panel that HAS such an object and leaves it unmarked is unfinished; a panel with NO cast-owned object needs no mark, and never add a prop just to carry the name. ABBY'S BAR TOWEL IS THE ONE EXCEPTION AND CARRIES NOTHING, EVER: plain white cloth, no name, no monogram, no woven mark, no lettering of any kind — a marked bar towel is a redraw.

THE BAR IS ONE LEVEL. COUNT THE HORIZONTAL MARBLE SURFACES: EXACTLY ONE — a single continuous flat slab of pale grey veined MARBLE at one height across the picture, walnut edge below. A second marble surface at ANY other height is a redraw. AND IT IS ONE STRAIGHT PLANE: where the marble shows beside a gentleman it lines up EXACTLY with the marble in front of him — one LEVEL top edge, parallel to the picture's bottom, frame-left to frame-right, never receding toward the window; a slab that steps up or tilts is a redraw. The back bar carries its bottles on HIGH SHELVES ONLY — the lowest shelf sits above the standing bartender's shoulders, plain fielded walnut panelling below.

THE SEATING IS THE SAME EVERY DAY: studded oxblood leather club chairs with brass nailheads along their backs. At most the top of a chair back shows behind each gentleman's own back at the frame's edge — never a seat, never a stool leg.

THE BAR HEIGHT IS FIXED, AND IT IS A TALL BAR — a real 42-inch counter, its top level with a seated man's mid-chest, never as low as his waist or belt. THE SLAB IS A SURFACE BEYOND HIM, NEVER A BAND DRAWN ACROSS HIM: no part of it overlaps, cuts across or passes through a gentleman's chest, waist, vest or jacket — his whole torso stands IN FRONT of the near edge and hides it, and only his forearms and his drink reach onto the top. A man with marble drawn across his body sits half sunk into the bar, and that is a redraw.

THE SIDES — absolute, and the thing this strip gets wrong most often. THE PROHIBITIONS FIRST: EXACTLY ONE counter, never a second counter, table, back ledge or work-top and never a nearer surface invented for the drinks; and the BACK BAR — bottles, mirror, television, chalkboard — stands ACROSS THE COUNTER on the FAR SERVICE SIDE with an EMPTY WALKWAY between the slab's far edge and its shelves — the shelves NEVER rise from the counter's edge and NEVER behind a gentleman's head. THE CAMERA is on the CUSTOMER SIDE, just behind and above the two gentlemen, looking ACROSS the one counter — one long slab of marble running LEFT TO RIGHT out of frame at both ends, never a wedge, never an island — to that back bar. DREW AND BARCLAY SIT AT ITS NEAR SIDE, close and large, SEEN FROM BEHIND and TURNED TOWARD EACH OTHER so each face reads in THREE-QUARTER over his own shoulder. THE GENTLEMEN ARE BETWEEN THE CAMERA AND THE COUNTER: each man's body BLOCKS the slab's near edge where he sits, so the marble shows only BETWEEN and BESIDE them at chest height — NEVER as an unbroken strip crossing in front of their chests. A gentleman the counter passes IN FRONT OF is standing in the bartender's place, and that is a redraw. AND WHEN ABBY IS NOT NAMED, THE FAR SERVICE SIDE HOLDS NO ONE — no bartender, no server, no second dog, no figure polishing a glass. COUNT THE FIGURES BEFORE YOU DRAW ANY OF THEM: this panel contains the characters this brief names and NOBODY ELSE, and inventing someone on the service side is a redraw.

NEAREST THE READER, DREW AND BARCLAY, SEATED AT THE COUNTER AND TURNED TOWARD EACH OTHER, seen FROM BEHIND from the customer side: Drew frame-LEFT, Barclay frame-RIGHT, each body turned only a quarter toward the other so the reader catches his face in THREE-QUARTER over his own shoulder. His own back and hip COVER the counter's near edge where he sits; the marble reaches the camera only beside and between the two of them, and the back bar stands far ACROSS it — never at his back. The BODY does the turning, so Barclay's far eye lands on the paper with no crank in his neck; Drew keeps his one-eyed profile, his head turned toward Barclay so the bill angles ACROSS the picture. Each man's chest still angles toward the marble, both forearms resting ON it and his drink on the slab in front of him, chest and shoulders rising CLEAR ABOVE its near edge. Nobody sits or perches ON the slab, and nobody hangs back from the bar he is drinking at.

NEXT, THE MARBLE COUNTER ITSELF, carrying Drew's martini, Barclay's old fashioned and the shared nut bowl side by side on its one surface, between and before the gentlemen where their hands can reach. THE COUNTER IS NEVER A STRIP ALONG THE BOTTOM OF THE FRAME WITH ALL THREE FIGURES BEHIND IT — that is what makes the gentlemen read as bartenders — and it is NEVER a table, a booth, a desk or a ledge: it is the bar's own slab, and the gentlemen are its patrons.

FARTHEST, PAST THE COUNTER, THE SERVICE SIDE: first the counter's FAR EDGE drawn as its own clean marble line beyond the drinks, then the walkway, then the back bar with its bottles and mirror, the television above it, the chalkboard beside — and ABBY when she is named, facing them, THE COUNTER'S FAR EDGE CROSSING HER AT THE WAIST and hiding her below it; she stands and they sit, so HER HEAD SITS HIGHER IN THE FRAME THAN THEIRS.

The two of them are on one side and she is on the other, always, and they never swap. When it is ambiguous the prop settles it: ANY LIQUOR BOTTLE OR BAR TOWEL IN THE PANEL IS ABBY'S — in her hands or on her shoulder — never in theirs. A stemmed glass has exactly ONE bowl on ONE stem on ONE foot — never a doubled stem, never two feet, never a second outline behind the hand. Every prop rests ON the marble or in a closed grip — nothing floats, nothing merges or clips. A LIFTED GLASS LEAVES ITS NAPKIN AND COASTER FLAT ON THE MARBLE: nothing sticks to the foot of a raised glass.

DREW. Preserve Drew exactly as the reference plates draw him (canon/vision/drew-plate1-bar-reference.jpg is the definitive study — the bar Drew of plate 1, with the LONG graceful high S-curve neck and the SMALL refined head; never a short thick neck, never a hunched or heavy bird. HIS BILL IS SLENDER, AND THE BLACK IS A MARKING ON IT RATHER THAN A PART OF IT. Two rules decide the shape, and they are the two the drawing keeps getting wrong.

FIRST, DEPTH. The bill is SLENDER: where it meets the feathers, its depth top-to-bottom is about ONE THIRD of its length. It tapers from there to the tip. Take the shape from a SWAN: a slender bill of even taper, bending in one gentle unbroken curve, with a small dark patch at the very tip. Its length is not the problem — a long slender bill is right; a thick one is wrong.

HIS BILL IS SLENDER AND IT DOES NOT BREAK. It leaves the face tucked and close, drops STEEPLY and STRAIGHT, and continues its own single curve smoothly to a ROUNDED TIP — one unbroken line from base to tip with no angle, no elbow, no kink and no hook anywhere along it. LAY A RULER ALONG THE UNDERSIDE AND IT SHOULD TOUCH ALMOST THE WHOLE LENGTH. The tip never hangs below the line the bill was already travelling on, and it never widens into a deep spoon. The rear two thirds are PALE; along the OUTER THIRD ONLY, the black IS the outline — it continues the bill's own curve rather than swelling into a bulb — with one bright highlight ribbon inside it. The NOSTRIL is a plain thin slit about HALF the length of his eye, with NO ring, outline or fleshy surround around it. There is no shelf or ridge above the eye.

He is FAR MORE FLAMINGO THAN HUMAN — plump, soft-bodied and FEATHERED ALL OVER in fine dash-strokes: breast, shoulders, back and arms, with long scalloped wing-feathers beneath each forearm. No human skin, torso, musculature or face anywhere; he is a bird who happens to sit at a bar. His neck is thick at the shoulders and rises in the deep question-mark sweep of a true flamingo, turning over at the top so the head hangs forward of where the neck left the body. His eyes are heavy-lidded and deadpan — visible white, distinct dark iris and pupil, a drooping upper lid and one fine contour line above it — never a bird dot. His face is AMIABLE: plump, softly modelled cheeks and a faint smile-line, a man who has heard it before and is fond of you anyway; never gaunt, hollow-eyed, sunken or sinister.

NO HAND IN THIS PANEL HAS A NAIL ON IT. Not Drew's, not Barclay's, not Abby's: every fingertip in the picture ends BLUNT AND SOFT in fur, plumage or pad, and a drawn nail, claw, talon or crescent at any fingertip is a redraw wherever it appears. THE ONLY HUMANLIKE THING ABOUT HIM IS HIS HANDS. Each feathered arm ends in a genuine hand — four slender fingers and an opposed thumb, feather-covered to the tips, elegant on a martini stem. WHITE PLUMAGE RUNS UNBROKEN FROM SHOULDER TO FINGERTIP: no sleeve, no cuff, no hem, no seam anywhere on the arm, and nothing smooth or bare-skinned anywhere on him. A crisp starched WHITE collar band circles the base of his neck and his small solid-black silk bow tie sits at the throat in front of it. DRAW THE TIE AS A TIED BOW: TWO wings of equal size spreading left and right, each wider at its outer edge, pinched to a SMALL CENTRE KNOT; horizontal, level, centred under the chin, resting ON the collar. Never one lump, never tilted, never more than two wings. THE BOW IS THE ONLY BLACK AT HIS NECK — no band, ribbon, strap, cord or choker runs around it or behind the bow. He wears a V-neck knitted sweater vest in fine honeycomb stitch with ribbed edges over a pale collared shirt, and trousers; THE VEST IS PLAIN KNIT WITH NO POCKETS ANYWHERE — none on the front, and never a pocket, flap or panel on the back. His plumage is pale but hatched — fine dash-strokes over white, high midtone rather than bare paper. At the bar his martini is always within reach: conical stemmed glass, ONE olive on ONE pick, on a napkin or coaster, held by the stem when lifted. His seat is frame-left, neck arched so his face hangs where the gag needs it. WHEN THIS SCENE HAS DREW SPEAKING his bill is SLIGHTLY PARTED, caught mid-word — never a clamped-shut bill on the one who is talking. At golf he adds a visor; a monocle is an approved occasional accessory.

BARCLAY. A successful gentleman in his mid-forties, unmistakably a golden retriever, drawn like one (canon/vision/barclay-reference.jpg is the definitive study): fur layered in fine individual strokes, drop ears with long fringe, broad soft-eyed retriever face, freckled muzzle, true black dog lips, dark lip-line along the muzzle from under his black nose, chest ruff modest, never a heavy neck-beard; middle-aged, solid, rounded shoulders, modest belly, absolutely no tail. HIS MOUTH IS CLOSED IN EVERY PANEL — never hanging open, never panting, never a visible tongue, never bared teeth. Default read: worried, earnest everyman against Drew's deadpan — BUT HE IS NOT SAD, and the first glance must not read as sad. Worry in the BROWS ONLY: raised inner brows, faint forehead wrinkle. Below the brows all WARM: mouth corners gently UP into a soft closed-lip smile, eyes bright and open, a clear catchlight in each, cheeks full and lifted. Read: a good-humoured man a little concerned, never a downcast one: mouth up, brows up, eyes bright. Hands visibly a dog's: broad, fur-backed, soft-padded fingers, NO NAILS OR CLAWS DRAWN AT ALL, each fingertip ending in soft fur and pad, never in a nail, yet fully humanoid in articulation: four fingers and an opposed thumb, believable human grips. At the bar, his dark suit jacket over a pale open-collared shirt, no tie; for daytime, travel, golf, a pale collared polo, dark leather belt, (outdoors) a ball cap; at golf his bag stands at frame-right, towel on its front hand-lettered in three lines FORE! / NOT SO / FAST. The small USA flag pin is PERMANENT: left lapel when jacketed, left chest of shirt or polo otherwise; on whatever he wears. A wristwatch on his left wrist in every panel EXCEPT at golf: a white golf glove on his left hand takes its place on that same wrist, smooth, unfurred to the cuff, forearm above it still furred; the watch and the glove are never both drawn, never on opposite sides of him. IN A BAR PANEL his old fashioned (short rocks glass, one large cube, one dark cherry) rests flat at frame-right, the shared bowl of bar nuts between the two drinks; AWAY FROM THE BAR he brings neither, whatever he holds belongs to the place he is in.

Drew and Barclay are gentlemen — classy, composed, well turned out; all three principals carry wisdom and command respect purely by how they carry themselves. Nothing about them is ever crude, sloppy or loud, and every scene carries that high-class read. Text inside the panel lives ON things and is a gag layer: whatever lettered surfaces THIS setting actually has — a chyron, a menu or scoreboard, a posted notice, a banner, a placard, a label — may each carry a short, legible, hand-lettered joke DRAWN FROM THE SAME JOKE as the caption, so the place and the line land as one gag from several angles. Letter ONLY the surfaces this setting genuinely has. No speech balloons, no thought bubbles, and no floating caption text inside the art — the dialogue is typeset by the house beneath the panel. THE SCENE: Barclay, earnest and resigned, swirls the ice in his old fashioned; Drew, deadpan, studies him over the rim of his martini; Abby, laughing, tops up the nut bowl in front of Barclay with a generous shake. IN THIS PANEL, CAMERA behind the two gentlemen on the CUSTOMER SIDE — their bodies block the counter's near edge — with ABBY working the FAR service side across the counter, the back bar behind HER alone. The television picture shows A gas pump with its nozzle hung in the cradle, the price display blank. Stage it exactly as THE SIDES describes. Abby is SMILING in this panel — an unmistakable smile, mouth corners up, eyes bright — NEVER sad, neutral or downcast; her beat is ACTIVE and cheerful: pouring, presenting a glass, laughing at her own line.

ABBY. Abby is the successful proprietor of The Swinging Door — a glamorous, feminine West Highland White Terrier in her mid-forties who owns the room and works its bar, drawn in the same engraved technique (canon/vision/abby-face-reference.jpg is the definitive face study): a true fluffy westie face in fine individual fur strokes, the head taken from a GROOMED SHOW WESTIE. HER FACE IS EXACTLY THE FACE OF HER STUDY, and wherever these words and that picture differ, THE PICTURE WINS. It is a small fluffy show-groomed head, ROUND AND SOFT: her big black nose sits DIRECTLY UNDER HER EYES on a round fluffy face — there is NO projecting muzzle to draw at all, no bridge, no cone, NO snout ever; nose, eyes and tiny closed smile all live on the front of one soft round head, and nothing sharp, foxish or wolfish appears anywhere. Her face reads SOFT, PRETTY, WARM and unmistakably FEMININE: long lashes, groomed brows, the fluff around her face shaped the way a stylist would leave it. HER EYES ARE HER BEST FEATURE AND THE MOST BEAUTIFUL THING IN THE PANEL. THEY ARE GLAMOROUS, LIDDED EYES, not a puppy's buttons: the upper lid sits low and sultry over the iris, the dark lash line is HEAVY and sweeps up and out at the corner, a bright catchlight sits high in each, and her look is warm, knowing and sidelong. Each is built like a HUMAN eye: a wide almond, WIDER THAN IT IS TALL, tilted up at the outer corner, white showing both sides of a drawn IRIS with a smaller round PUPIL. Draw them LARGE — EACH EYE AT LEAST AS WIDE AS THE BLACK OF HER NOSE — clear, bright and alert. Two or three fine brow strokes above each, two small pricked ears, and A SMILE IN EVERY PANEL — an unmistakable smile, mouth corners clearly UP and eyes bright, closed-lip or a happy open smile, whether she is at rest, serving or landing a line; a straight, neutral, pursed or downcast mouth on her is a redraw, as are drooping brows or mournful eyes. She is turned into the frame only as far as keeps BOTH EYES ON THE PAPER, the far eye at least half the width of the near one, the bridge of her muzzle showing between them. Her body is slightly humanoid, built exactly like the two gentlemen: upright on two legs, humanoid shoulders and arms, and fur-backed dog-yet-humanoid hands with soft pads and FOUR FINGERS AND AN OPPOSED THUMB, every finger separately drawn, closing on glass, towel and bottle neck in believable human grips. Trim, natural and graceful: a clean shoulder line and a waist the reader can find. HER FIGURE IS SLIM AND HER BUST IS SMALL AND NATURAL — the placket of her blouse runs very nearly STRAIGHT DOWN her front and the front reads as one gentle plane, never two separated volumes with a shadowed cleft between them. Her blouse is UNBUTTONED TWO BUTTONS DOWN so the collar falls open in a soft V, and the V falls open DEEP ENOUGH THAT THE SMOOTH CURVE OF HER CLEAVAGE SHOWS, drawn frankly attractive: throat, collarbone and the soft shadowed line between the curves, all reading as smooth skin. THE FUR IS WHAT SPOILS IT, so the long fur of her head and cheeks STOPS at her jawline and below it everything is SHORT, FINE and CLOSE-LYING — not one ruff, tuft or wisp of fluff breaks the clean line of the V. It is a LOWER NECKLINE, never a larger bust, and a shaggy chest inside an open collar is a redraw. She wears her fitted light blouse with rolled sleeves, a dark fitted skirt, a studded leather collar with a small teardrop gem pendant at its centre, a pearl bracelet and black heels; absolutely no tail. Her folded bar towel is ALWAYS SOMEWHERE IN THE PANEL, never missing from it, and in EXACTLY ONE PLACE AND NEVER BOTH: either draped over her LEFT SHOULDER with both hands empty of it, or held in her hands round the glass she is polishing with her shoulder BARE. There is only one towel in the panel. IN A BAR PANEL she works the service side directly across the marble from the gentlemen, standing to it on her own two feet with her arms free, visibly mid-task with ONE HAND CLOSED ON A WORKING OBJECT — glass, bottle, towel, chalk, or whatever THIS scene hands her; when the scene gives her its own object to handle, the towel rides her LEFT SHOULDER and both hands stay free of it — and the panel crops at the counter, its far edge cutting her at the waist and hiding her below it. AWAY FROM THE BAR she stands on the ground like everyone else, there on a named errand of the house, still with her towel and still with one hand busy, with no counter to stand behind, and the panel crops at whatever edge that setting names.
